title: The Saddle Point: Up One Way, Down the Other
topic: At the origin of z = x² − y² the gradient vanishes, but it is no extremum. Rotate a cutting plane through the centre: the cross-section z = r²·cos(2φ) morphs from an upward parabola (a valley, φ = 0) through flat (φ = 45°) to a downward parabola (a ridge, φ = 90°). Opposite curvature in the two principal directions means Hesse eigenvalues of opposite sign and discriminant D < 0 — the signature of a saddle.

beats.narration: The ground is perfectly flat here, yet it is neither a hilltop nor the bottom of a valley.

elements.content: Flat ground — but no peak and no pit. What is this?

beats.narration: Take the surface z equals x squared minus y squared. At the origin the gradient is zero, so it is a critical point — but the surface curves up along one axis and down along the other.

beats.narration: Spin a cutting plane through the centre. Along one direction the slice is a valley that curves upward; rotate by ninety degrees and it becomes a ridge that curves downward; halfway between, the slice is perfectly flat.
